exclusive

/ik-SKLOO-siv/ — stress on SKLOO · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something exclusive is limited to a select few people because it is expensive, high-status, or closed to the general public.

The chef opened an exclusive dining room with just six tables, booked a year ahead.

Worked Example

The country club kept its membership exclusive, turning away applicants who weren't referred by a current member.

Exclus (from exclude) + -ive: The root exclud- comes from Latin exclusus, 'shut out.' The -ive suffix means 'inclined to, having the quality of.' So exclusive literally means 'inclined to shut others out.' In social and commercial contexts, this evolved into 'reserved for a select few with special status or access.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

elite: Elite names the group at the top — an elite squad or elite school is made of the best or most privileged members. Exclusive describes the barrier around something: it is closed to all but a chosen few. An elite team is defined by who is in it; an exclusive one by who is kept out.

prestigious: Prestigious means widely admired and high in status — a prestigious award or university carries honor. Exclusive is about access, not admiration: it shuts most people out. A prestigious prize can be open to any entrant, while an exclusive club might be little known and still bar nearly everyone.

privileged: Privileged means enjoying special advantages most people lack, or reserved for those who do — privileged information, a privileged upbringing. Exclusive points at the thing doing the excluding: the club, list, or shop that admits only a favored few and turns the rest of the world away.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

inclusive: welcoming everyone in

open: available to anyone at all

Where it sits · how few people are let in — private → selective → restricted → exclusive

private vs. exclusive: 'Private' just means not public, while exclusive shuts out everyone but a chosen few.

selective vs. exclusive: A selective club turns some people away; an exclusive one admits only a tiny, favored circle.

restricted vs. exclusive: 'Restricted' limits entry by rule, but exclusive is stronger, reserving something for a select elite.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — exclus-

Root — exclus-: shifted stem of exclude — from Latin excludere, 'to shut out' (past participle exclusus) (Latin)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: having the quality or tendency of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Exclude swaps its -de ending for -s- (Latin exclusus) before -ive: inclined to shut others out — something limited to a chosen few.

Use the root in a new word: exclusivity

Use the root in a new word: exclusivity: The sneaker brand built its fame on exclusivity, releasing only five hundred pairs.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / aspirational

Reach for exclusive when you want to convey both restriction and prestige or high value — something not only limited but desirable. For mere limitation without status, use restricted or off-limits. For a group with superior status, elite is more direct.
